Let’s talk about something that can truly shift your experience— mindfulness.
Welcome to Chapter 2: The Power of Mindfulness—Shifting from Doing to Being.
Most of us, when we feel emotionally distressed, try to change our thoughts or fix our circumstances. And honestly, that can help. But have you ever wondered if there’s another way? What if you could change your entire relationship with thoughts and feelings, instead of just fighting them? That’s where mindfulness steps in.
Mindfulness isn’t about clearing your mind or finding a state of perfect calm. It’s about noticing whatever’s happening—good or bad—without instantly trying to change it.
Here’s the thing: our minds usually run in “doing” mode. We’re always evaluating, comparing, striving. But when we shift into “being” mode, something changes. There’s space to simply notice and accept what’s here, right now.
Picture yourself walking through a park. In “doing” mode, maybe you’re focused on getting somewhere, planning your next move, or replaying an argument in your head. But if you step into “being” mode, suddenly you notice the rustle of leaves, the warmth of the sun, the sound of birds overhead. That kind of awareness? It’s always available—even when life feels tough.
Mindfulness gives us a way to step back from our automatic reactions. It helps us see thoughts for what they are—just mental events, not facts. So when a thought like, “I’m a failure,” pops up, you can recognize it as just that—a thought. Not the truth. That little bit of distance? It can make all the difference.
The more you practice mindfulness, the stronger this skill becomes. Over time, you’ll notice those early signs of low mood or negative thinking, and you’ll have more options in how you respond. Instead of being swept away by your thoughts, you learn to stand on the riverbank and watch them flow past.
Here are a few simple ways to practice mindfulness:
First, there’s breath awareness—just gently focus on your breathing, noticing each inhale and exhale.
Then, try a body scan: slowly move your attention through your body, noticing any sensations, without judgment.
Or give mindful walking a go. Pay close attention to each step, the movement of your body, and everything around you.
Remember, these practices aren’t about getting rid of tough feelings. They’re about creating space around them—giving you an anchor to return to, even when your mind feels stormy.
So, here’s what really matters:
Mindfulness means paying attention to the present moment with openness and curiosity.
Shifting from “doing” to “being” opens up a whole new relationship with your thoughts and feelings.
Practicing mindfulness interrupts those automatic reactions and gives you room to choose your response.
And with regular practice, you’ll build greater resilience and flexibility, even in the face of emotional challenges.
